# How the exam asks, and exam English: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=how-the-exam-asks-q004 -->
### Question 1

A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets in two Availability Zones. The instances currently send large uploads to an Amazon S3 bucket in the same AWS Region through one NAT gateway. The uploads come only from the instances in the VPC. The uploads must reach Amazon S3 privately, and the company wants to reduce the NAT gateway data processing charges. What is the MOST cost-effective solution that meets these requirements?

- Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, and add a route to the endpoint in the route table of each private subnet.
- Create an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, with an endpoint network interface in a private subnet in each Availability Zone.
- Create an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 in each Availability Zone, and add a second NAT gateway so that each zone has its own.
- Move the instances to public subnets, assign public IP addresses, and send the uploads to Amazon S3 through an internet gateway.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, and add a route to the endpoint in the route table of each private subnet.

**Deciding phrases.** "come only from the instances in the VPC", "reach Amazon S3 privately", "MOST cost-effective"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the MOST cost-effective solution that meets every requirement.
2. I mark the constraints: the uploads go to Amazon S3 in the same Region, they come only from the instances in the VPC, they must reach Amazon S3 privately, and the NAT gateway data processing charge is the cost to cut.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, because it keeps the traffic off the internet and has no hourly or data processing charge.
4. I remove the move to public subnets, because an internet gateway sends the uploads over the internet. I remove the option with a second NAT gateway, because it adds a charge that the uploads do not need.
5. Between the gateway endpoint and the interface endpoint the difference is cost; the stem says the uploads come only from the instances in the VPC, so both endpoints work, and the gateway endpoint has no hourly charge.
6. Check: the gateway endpoint meets every constraint and removes the NAT gateway data processing charge for the uploads. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** Both endpoint types keep the uploads private, so the word privately does not decide. The cost qualifier does: [there are no data processing or hourly charges for using Gateway Type VPC endpoints](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-hourly-or-processing-charge), and routing the uploads through the gateway endpoint lets the company [avoid the NAT Gateway Data Processing charge](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-hourly-or-processing-charge).

**Why not.**

- "Create an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, ...": One endpoint per zone is private too, but an interface endpoint is [billed for each hour that your interface VPC endpoint is provisioned in each Availability Zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-interface-endpoint-billed-hour-per-az-and-gb).
- "Create an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 ...": The endpoint plus a second NAT gateway works, but the interface endpoint and the extra NAT gateway add hourly charges that the uploads do not need.
- "Move the instances to public subnets, assign public ...": An internet gateway sends the uploads over the internet, so the uploads do not reach Amazon S3 privately.

**Twin.** If the stem said "servers in the company's data center" instead: an interface endpoint, because [gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks, from peered VPCs in other AWS Regions, or through a transit gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-onprem-cross-region-tgw).

**Takeaway.** Private is a requirement that both endpoints meet; the cost qualifier then picks the gateway endpoint.

**Review.** [Optimisation qualifiers](2-deep.md#optimisation-qualifiers-2-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets in two Availability Zones. The instances currently send large uploads to an Amazon S3 bucket in the same AWS Region through one NAT gateway. The uploads also come from servers in the company's data center, which connect to the VPC over an AWS Direct Connect private virtual interface. All uploads must reach Amazon S3 privately through the VPC, and the company wants to reduce the NAT gateway data processing charges. What is the MOST cost-effective solution that meets these requirements?

- Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, and add a route to the endpoint in the route table of each private subnet.
- Create an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, with an endpoint network interface in a private subnet in each Availability Zone.
- Create an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 in each Availability Zone, and add a second NAT gateway so that each zone has its own.
- Move the instances to public subnets, assign public IP addresses, and send the uploads to Amazon S3 through an internet gateway.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, with an endpoint network interface in a private subnet in each Availability Zone.

**Deciding phrases.** "also come from servers in the company's data center", "reach Amazon S3 privately", "MOST cost-effective"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the MOST cost-effective solution that meets every requirement.
2. I mark the constraints: the uploads come from the instances and from servers in the data center over a Direct Connect private virtual interface, they must reach Amazon S3 privately through the VPC, and the NAT gateway data processing charge is the cost to cut.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, because it has no hourly or data processing charge.
4. I remove the move to public subnets, because an internet gateway sends the uploads over the internet. I remove the option with a second NAT gateway, because it adds a charge that the uploads do not need.
5. Between the gateway endpoint and the interface endpoint the difference is who can use the endpoint. My first idea breaks because gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks, and the stem says the data center also uploads. So I choose the interface endpoint, which supports connectivity over Direct Connect.
6. Check: the interface endpoint meets every constraint for both sources of uploads, and it removes the NAT gateway charge for them. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** The cheapest endpoint fails one requirement, because [gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks, from peered VPCs in other AWS Regions, or through a transit gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-onprem-cross-region-tgw). For that case [you must use an interface endpoint, which is available for an additional cost](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-onprem-cross-region-tgw). The qualifier then ranks what is left, and the interface endpoint without an extra NAT gateway costs least.

**Why not.**

- "Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, ...": It is the cheapest, but [gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks, from peered VPCs in other AWS Regions, or through a transit gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-onprem-cross-region-tgw).
- "Create an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 ...": The endpoint plus a second NAT gateway works, but the extra NAT gateway adds an hourly charge that the private uploads do not need.
- "Move the instances to public subnets, assign public ...": An internet gateway sends the uploads over the internet, so the uploads do not reach Amazon S3 privately.

**Twin.** If the stem said "come only from the instances in the VPC" instead: a gateway endpoint, because [there are no data processing or hourly charges for using Gateway Type VPC endpoints](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-hourly-or-processing-charge).

**Takeaway.** The cheapest option is out when it fails one requirement; then rank the options that remain.

</details>

### Question 3

A company runs a web application on four Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer in one AWS Region. The VPC has subnets across multiple Availability Zones, but all four instances run in the same Availability Zone. Last month, a failure in that Availability Zone stopped the application for two hours. The application must be highly available and must keep serving requests if one Availability Zone fails. What should a solutions architect do?

- Replace the four instances with two larger instances in the same Availability Zone, so that each instance can carry the whole load.
- Launch the instances across subnets in two Availability Zones, and register the instances in both zones with the load balancer.
- Take daily snapshots of the instance volumes, and restore the instances from the snapshots in another Availability Zone after a failure.
- Create an Auto Scaling group in the current Availability Zone that replaces each unhealthy instance with a new instance in that zone.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Launch the instances across subnets in two Availability Zones, and register the instances in both zones with the load balancer.

**Deciding phrases.** "all four instances run in the same Availability Zone", "keep serving requests if one Availability Zone fails"

**Why.** The stem names one failure: the loss of one Availability Zone. When every instance runs in that zone, [none of your EC2 instances would be available](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-single-az-failure-takes-all-instances) after a zone failure. AWS recommends [at least two Availability Zones](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-prod-at-least-two-azs) for production, so the answer spreads the instances across two zones behind the load balancer.

**Why not.**

- "Replace the four instances with two larger instances ...": Larger instances add capacity, not zones: if that zone fails, [none of your EC2 instances would be available](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-single-az-failure-takes-all-instances).
- "Take daily snapshots of the instance volumes, and ...": A snapshot is a backup, not a running copy, so the application stays down while someone restores the instances.
- "Create an Auto Scaling group in the current ...": The group replaces instances inside the same zone, and when that zone fails, [none of your EC2 instances would be available](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-single-az-failure-takes-all-instances).

**Twin.** If the stem said "must keep serving requests if the whole Region fails" instead: a design in a second Region, because each Region is [designed to be isolated from the other Regions](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-region-isolated-for-fault-tolerance).

**Takeaway.** Find the failure that the stem names, then choose the design that survives exactly that failure.

**Review.** [Location and network](2-deep.md#location-and-network-2-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company runs workloads on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets in three Availability Zones of one VPC. Each private subnet has its own route table. The instances download software updates from a vendor's website on the internet, and the traffic volume is small. The instances must not have public IP addresses. If one Availability Zone fails, an interruption of internet access is acceptable. What is the MOST cost-effective solution that meets these requirements?

- Create one NAT gateway in a public subnet in one Availability Zone, and point the default route of every private route table to that NAT gateway.
- Create one NAT gateway in a public subnet in each Availability Zone, and point the default route of each private route table to the NAT gateway in its zone.
- Create two NAT gateways in public subnets in each Availability Zone, and point the default route of each private route table to one NAT gateway in its zone.
- Assign a public IP address to each instance, and point the default route of each private route table to the internet gateway of the VPC.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create one NAT gateway in a public subnet in one Availability Zone, and point the default route of every private route table to that NAT gateway.

**Deciding phrases.** "an interruption of internet access is acceptable", "must not have public IP addresses", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** Three options give the instances internet access without public IP addresses. The stem accepts an interruption if one zone fails, so the qualifier decides. NAT gateways are [charged depending on the number of NAT gateways you use, duration of usage, and amount of data that you send through the NAT gateways](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-vs-instance-cost), and the traffic is small, so one shared gateway costs least.

**Why not.**

- "Create one NAT gateway in a public subnet ...": One gateway in each zone works, but the stem accepts an interruption, and three gateways cost more than one because the number of gateways is billed.
- "Create two NAT gateways in public subnets in ...": It works, but [each NAT gateway is created in a specific Availability Zone and implemented with redundancy in that zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-one-az-redundant-in-zone), so a second one adds cost.
- "Assign a public IP address to each instance, ...": The stem forbids public IP addresses on the instances, so this design breaks a stated requirement at any price.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Internet access must continue if one Availability Zone fails" instead: one NAT gateway in each zone, because otherwise [resources in the other Availability Zones lose internet access](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-shared-across-azs-loses-internet).

**Takeaway.** When the stem accepts an interruption, the cheaper design that still meets every requirement wins.

**Review.** [Exam English core words](1-fast.md#exam-english-core-words-2-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A company uses AWS Organizations and has 30 member accounts. Its 200 employees sign in to company applications through the company's existing identity provider. Each employee needs access to a different set of accounts. The security team wants to centrally manage this access from one place, and employees must use temporary credentials in the accounts. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create IAM users with the same names in each member account, and require the employees to rotate the access keys of those users on a schedule.
- Create an IAM role in each member account that trusts the identity provider through SAML federation, and update the roles in every account by hand.
- Connect the identity provider to IAM Identity Center, create permission sets, and assign groups of employees to the accounts that they need.
- Create one IAM user in the management account for all employees, share its password, and let the employees switch roles into member accounts.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Connect the identity provider to IAM Identity Center, create permission sets, and assign groups of employees to the accounts that they need.

**Deciding phrases.** "centrally manage this access", "must use temporary credentials", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Several options give access, and the qualifier ranks the ones that work. AWS calls IAM Identity Center its [recommended front door into AWS](../facts/iam.md#iam-idc-recommended-front-door-for-workforce) for workforce users. The team connects the existing identity provider once and assigns permission sets, and employees receive role credentials in each account instead of user keys.

**Why not.**

- "Create IAM users with the same names in ...": [IAM users have long-term credentials such as passwords and access keys](../facts/iam.md#iam-users-have-long-term-credentials-roles-do-not), so rotating the keys does not make the credentials temporary.
- "Create an IAM role in each member account ...": It works, but the team creates and updates a role in every account by hand, work that IAM Identity Center does for each permission set.
- "Create one IAM user in the management account ...": One shared user gives every employee the same access, so the employees do not get different sets of accounts.

**Twin.** If the stem said "an application on Amazon EC2 instances needs access" instead: an IAM role for the instances, because [AWS delivers the temporary credentials of an IAM role to that compute resource](../facts/iam.md#iam-compute-services-receive-role-credentials-no-keys-needed).

**Takeaway.** Workforce access to many accounts with the least work: IAM Identity Center with permission sets.

**Review.** [Exam English core words](1-fast.md#exam-english-core-words-2-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 6

A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets in two Availability Zones. The instances call a partner's API on the internet. A small team operates the AWS environment and does not want to patch or replace network devices. The instances must not have public IP addresses, and internet access for the instances must be highly available. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Launch a NAT instance in a public subnet in each Availability Zone, and run a script that moves the routes to a healthy NAT instance after a failure.
- Attach an internet gateway to the VPC, assign a public IP address to each instance, and route the private subnets to the internet gateway.
- Create a gateway VPC endpoint, add it to the route table of each private subnet, and send the partner API traffic to the endpoint.
- Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet in each Availability Zone, and route each private subnet to the NAT gateway in its own zone.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet in each Availability Zone, and route each private subnet to the NAT gateway in its own zone.

**Deciding phrases.** "A small team", "does not want to patch", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Two options give the instances highly available internet access without public IP addresses: NAT gateways, and NAT instances with a failover script. The qualifier ranks them. A NAT instance needs you to [use a script to manage failover between instances](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-vs-instance-availability) and to patch it, while a NAT gateway is [managed by AWS](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-vs-instance-maintenance).

**Why not.**

- "Launch a NAT instance in a public subnet ...": It works, but a NAT instance is [managed by you, for example, by installing software updates or operating system patches on the instance](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-vs-instance-maintenance), which the team wants to avoid.
- "Attach an internet gateway to the VPC, assign ...": The stem forbids public IP addresses on the instances, so a route to an internet gateway breaks a stated requirement.
- "Create a gateway VPC endpoint, add it to ...": [Gateway VPC endpoints provide reliable connectivity to Amazon S3 and DynamoDB without requiring an internet gateway or a NAT device for your VPC](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-s3-dynamodb-no-privatelink); a partner API is not one of them.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the instances call Amazon S3" instead: a gateway endpoint, because [Gateway VPC endpoints provide reliable connectivity to Amazon S3 and DynamoDB without requiring an internet gateway or a NAT device for your VPC](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-s3-dynamodb-no-privatelink).

**Takeaway.** A small team and LEAST operational overhead: choose the managed device over the one you patch.

**Review.** [Read the stem in this order](1-fast.md#read-the-stem-in-this-order-2-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 7

A company runs workloads on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets in three Availability Zones of one VPC. Each private subnet has its own route table. The instances download software updates from a vendor's website on the internet, and the traffic volume is small. The instances must not have public IP addresses. Internet access must continue if one Availability Zone fails. What is the MOST cost-effective solution that meets these requirements?

- Create one NAT gateway in a public subnet in one Availability Zone, and point the default route of every private route table to that NAT gateway.
- Create one NAT gateway in a public subnet in each Availability Zone, and point the default route of each private route table to the NAT gateway in its zone.
- Create two NAT gateways in public subnets in each Availability Zone, and point the default route of each private route table to one NAT gateway in its zone.
- Assign a public IP address to each instance, and point the default route of each private route table to the internet gateway of the VPC.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create one NAT gateway in a public subnet in each Availability Zone, and point the default route of each private route table to the NAT gateway in its zone.

**Deciding phrases.** "Internet access must continue if one Availability Zone fails", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The stem requires internet access to continue when one zone fails. A shared gateway is the cheapest design, but it breaks that requirement, so it is removed before the qualifier ranks. Of the designs that work, one gateway in each zone costs less than two, because NAT gateways are [charged depending on the number of NAT gateways you use, duration of usage, and amount of data that you send through the NAT gateways](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-vs-instance-cost).

**Why not.**

- "Create one NAT gateway in a public subnet ...": One gateway in one zone is the cheapest, but if its zone fails, [resources in the other Availability Zones lose internet access](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-shared-across-azs-loses-internet), which breaks the requirement.
- "Create two NAT gateways in public subnets in ...": It works, but [each NAT gateway is created in a specific Availability Zone and implemented with redundancy in that zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-one-az-redundant-in-zone), so a second one adds cost.
- "Assign a public IP address to each instance, ...": The stem forbids public IP addresses on the instances, so this design breaks a stated requirement at any price.

**Twin.** If the stem said "an interruption of internet access is acceptable" instead: one shared NAT gateway, because the designs with more gateways cost more and the interruption is allowed.

**Takeaway.** A hard requirement removes the cheapest design first; then the qualifier ranks what is left.

### Question 8

A company runs a reporting application on Amazon EC2 instances. The application reads objects from one Amazon S3 bucket by using the access key of an IAM user. The key is stored in a configuration file on each instance. A new company policy requires that no long-term credentials are stored on the instances and that the application has least privilege. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Run a scheduled script that rotates the access key of the IAM user every week and copies the new key into the file on each instance.
- Create an IAM role with a policy that allows read actions on the objects in that one bucket, and let Amazon EC2 assume the role.
- Create an IAM role with the AdministratorAccess managed policy, so that the application keeps working when it later needs other AWS services.
- Attach the role to the instances through an instance profile, and delete the access key and the configuration file from each instance.
- Create a separate IAM role for each instance, each with its own copy of the read policy, and attach each role to its own instance.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create an IAM role with a policy that allows read actions on the objects in that one bucket, and let Amazon EC2 assume the role.
- Attach the role to the instances through an instance profile, and delete the access key and the configuration file from each instance.

**Deciding phrases.** "no long-term credentials are stored on the instances", "least privilege", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Each correct step is right on its own, and the two work together. The role replaces the stored key, and role credentials on EC2 are [temporary and updated automatically](../facts/iam.md#iam-ec2-role-credentials-rotate-automatically), so the team does not rotate or store them.

- A role [does not have standard long-term credentials, such as a password or access keys](../facts/iam.md#iam-users-have-long-term-credentials-roles-do-not), and one bucket keeps least privilege.
- Through the instance profile, [AWS delivers the temporary credentials of an IAM role to that compute resource](../facts/iam.md#iam-compute-services-receive-role-credentials-no-keys-needed), so the stored key can go.

**Why not.**

- "Run a scheduled script that rotates the access ...": A rotated key is still an access key, and access keys [remain valid until you manually revoke them](../facts/iam.md#iam-long-term-keys-valid-until-revoked-temporary-expire).
- "Create an IAM role with the AdministratorAccess managed ...": AdministratorAccess gives far more than reading one bucket, and least privilege means [defining the actions that can be taken on specific resources under specific conditions](../facts/iam.md#iam-best-practice-least-privilege-definition).
- "Create a separate IAM role for each instance, ...": It works, but one shared role serves every instance, and a change to that role [propagates to all of them](../facts/iam.md#iam-ec2-role-credentials-rotate-automatically); separate roles multiply the work.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the application runs as an AWS Lambda function" instead: the function's execution role, because [AWS delivers the temporary credentials of an IAM role to that compute resource](../facts/iam.md#iam-compute-services-receive-role-credentials-no-keys-needed).

**Takeaway.** Judge each option alone, then check that the chosen steps work together as one solution.

**Review.** [Multiple-response questions](1-fast.md#multiple-response-questions-1-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets behind an Application Load Balancer in public subnets. The load balancer and the instances have separate security groups. The security team must block one abusive public IP address range in the subnets of the load balancer. The team must also ensure that the instances accept HTTPS traffic from the load balancer only and restrict all other inbound traffic. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Add an inbound deny rule for the address range to the network ACL of the load balancer's subnets, with a lower rule number than the allow rules.
- Add an inbound deny rule for the address range to the security group of the load balancer, and keep its existing allow rule for HTTPS.
- Add an inbound deny rule for the address range to the network ACL of every subnet in the VPC, and repeat the rule for each new subnet.
- Change the security group of the instances to allow HTTPS from 0.0.0.0/0, and rely on the network ACL rule to stop the abusive range.
- Change the security group of the instances to allow HTTPS from the security group of the load balancer, and remove all other inbound rules.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Add an inbound deny rule for the address range to the network ACL of the load balancer's subnets, with a lower rule number than the allow rules.
- Change the security group of the instances to allow HTTPS from the security group of the load balancer, and remove all other inbound rules.

**Deciding phrases.** "block one abusive public IP address range", "accept HTTPS traffic from the load balancer only", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Two requirements need two steps, and each correct option meets one of them on its own. Blocking an address range needs a deny rule, and [network ACLs can be used to set both Allow and Deny rules](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-allow-rules-only). Limiting the instances to load balancer traffic is a security group rule that names the security group of the load balancer.

- Network ACL rules are evaluated [starting with the lowest numbered rule](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-nacl-rule-order-first-match), so the deny rule stops the range before an allow rule matches.
- As in the AWS example, the instance security group [allows inbound HTTPS access from the load balancer](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-chain-web-allows-lb-sg) by naming the load balancer's security group.

**Why not.**

- "Add an inbound deny rule for the address ...": A deny rule in the security group cannot exist: in a security group, [you can specify allow rules, but not deny rules](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-allow-rules-only).
- "Add an inbound deny rule for the address ...": A deny rule in every subnet's network ACL works, but the team maintains it everywhere, although the traffic enters through the load balancer's subnets.
- "Change the security group of the instances to ...": An allow rule from 0.0.0.0/0 lets any address reach the instances on HTTPS, which breaks the second requirement of the stem.

**Twin.** If the stem said "allow HTTPS from one partner address range" instead: an allow rule in the security group, because that stem needs no deny rule.

**Takeaway.** Two requirements, two steps: each correct option meets one requirement on its own.

**Review.** [Multiple-response questions](1-fast.md#multiple-response-questions-1-min)

</details>

### Question 10

A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled and has 40 member accounts. Each member account sends VPC flow logs to a central log archive. Administrators in the member accounts have full IAM permissions in their own accounts. The security team must ensure that no one in the member accounts, including the root user, can delete the flow logs of their VPCs. The team wants to centrally manage this control. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create an Amazon EventBridge rule in each member account that sends an alert to the security team when someone deletes a flow log.
- Attach an identity-based policy that denies the deletion of flow logs to every IAM user and every IAM role in the member accounts.
- Create an SCP that denies the deletion of flow logs, and attach the SCP to each member account in the organization one account at a time.
- Create an SCP that denies the deletion of flow logs, and attach the SCP once to the root of the organization in AWS Organizations.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an SCP that denies the deletion of flow logs, and attach the SCP once to the root of the organization in AWS Organizations.

**Deciding phrases.** "must ensure", "including the root user", "centrally manage this control"

**Why.** The stem asks for a control that stops the deletion, and the strongest principal in the stem is the root user. An SCP [restricts permissions for IAM users and roles in member accounts](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-applies-to-member-root-user), [including the member account's root user](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-applies-to-member-root-user), and member principals [cannot remove or change SCPs that are applied to that account](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-faq-member-principals-cannot-change-scps). Attached [to the root of your organization](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-faq-attach-at-root-ou-or-account), one SCP covers every member account.

**Why not.**

- "Create an Amazon EventBridge rule in each member ...": An alert reports a deletion after it happens, but the stem asks for a control that stops the deletion itself.
- "Attach an identity-based policy that denies the deletion ...": Administrators can detach the policy, and you [cannot attach identity-based policies to the root user](../facts/iam.md#iam-root-user-no-identity-policies-or-boundary).
- "Create an SCP that denies the deletion of ...": Attaching the SCP account by account works, but it is more work than one attachment at the root of the organization.

**Twin.** If the stem said "wants to be notified when someone deletes a flow log" instead: the EventBridge alert, because that stem asks for detection, not prevention.

**Takeaway.** When the stem forbids an action for every principal, root user included, choose a deny SCP, not an alert or an IAM policy.

**Review.** [Exam English core words](1-fast.md#exam-english-core-words-2-min)

</details>
